strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem setting: KV cache eviction for long reasoning generations is an important and timely efficiency problem, and the empirical study (Section 2) provides genuine insight—categorizing attention patterns into global/position-dependent/semantic-dependent types and demonstrating the disproportionate loss increase on low-entropy tokens after eviction (Table 1).

The two-stage design is sensible and well-justified: the Golden Eviction algorithm provides future-aware supervision labels, addressing a real weakness of single-pass heuristics like SnapKV, and the RL stage (GRPO over an MDP formulation) addresses the distribution shift between the supervised label construction and actual inference-time eviction states. The ablation showing supervised-only vs. supervised+RL (Figure 3) confirms both stages contribute.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix A (error bound proportional to evicted attention mass, extended to future-block surrogates) gives a principled connection between the Golden Eviction objective and generation quality preservation.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: three model families, two main benchmarks with 32 samples per configuration (pass@1 averaging), multiple budget settings, throughput/batch-size measurements (Table 3), end-to-end speed analysis (Appendix E.9), ablations on scoring-model inputs and sampling (Table 5), five reward variants (Table 4), entropy-threshold sensitivity (Table 10), additional baselines (G-KV, DuoAttention, RPC in Table 17), scaling to Qwen3-14B/32B, and transfer to MiniCPM and non-math tasks (GPQA, LiveCodeBench, LongBench).

Practical efficiency results are compelling: near-full performance at half the cache budget across models, up to 9.79x throughput gain at 32K generation, and eviction overhead of only 2.7% of total time.
Training details, hyperparameters, and training cost (Appendix E.1) are reported, and code is stated to be available, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The method is training-based and per-model: a separate scoring model must be trained for each LLM using that model's own reasoning traces. While lightweight (MLP scorers, ~14h total on 8 GPUs for the largest model), this limits plug-and-play applicability relative to training-free baselines, and the paper does not quantify how performance degrades when a scoring model trained on one backbone is applied to another.

Golden Eviction is a heuristic oracle: it minimizes future attention mass under a max-pooling surrogate, which is a reasonable but crude proxy for actual generation quality. The Appendix A bound is straightforward (triangle inequality on bounded value vectors) and the local-Lipschitz assumptions linking attention perturbation to token loss are stated but not empirically validated.

The low-entropy reward design introduces several hyperparameters (entropy percentile, loss threshold eta, margin) whose selection is only partially justified; the sensitivity analysis covers the entropy threshold but not eta or the 1.5 threshold in the margin condition.

The core empirical study in Section 2.1 (attention pattern taxonomy) rests on visualization of a single representative response and one model, making the qualitative claims about 'semantic-dependent' patterns somewhat anecdotal, though Appendix C partially compensates with quantitative cosine-similarity evidence.

Evaluation is heavily centered on math reasoning (AIME 2024/2025); the generalization experiments (GPQA, LiveCodeBench, LongBench) are welcome but use small budgets and fewer settings, and the RL stage is trained only on math traces, so cross-domain RL benefits are not fully characterized.

Comparison against other trained eviction methods is thin: Locret (Huang et al., 2024) and attention-gate (Zeng et al., 2024) are discussed as closely related training-based approaches but are not included as baselines in the main comparison.
Statistical reporting could be stronger: AIME has few problems (30/year) and while averaging over 32 runs helps, no confidence intervals or significance tests are provided for the reported gaps.
